"""
A durable append-only event journal with framing, checksums, recovery,
filtering, and an atomic index rebuild.

Design overview
---------------
The journal writes each event as a *frame*:

    [magic(4)] [length(8, big-endian)] [payload(N)] [crc32(4)] [len_field_crc(4)]

Invariants (enforced by the code and by the tests):

  INV1. Every frame starts with MAGIC_MARKER. On recovery, we only trust a
        frame that begins with the magic bytes.
  INV2. `length` is the exact byte length of the encoded payload, and the
        subsequent payload+crc bytes are contiguous (no gaps).
  INV3. crc32 is computed over the *payload only*. That way, the checksum does
        not depend on the framing length, which simplifies recovery of frames
        whose tail was partially written (we can still detect truncation by
        comparing declared length against remaining bytes).
  INV4. length_field_crc32 is computed over the 8-byte length field bytes plus
        the payload length value shifted (i.e. over (length_bytes)). This is a
        belt-and-suspenders guard: a corrupted length field is caught before we
        try to allocate/slice with a wrong length.
  INV5. A frame is only considered *durable* after `append()` returns, which
        implies the file was flushed to the OS (and optionally fsync'ed to disk).
  INV6. A truncated tail (a frame that started but did not finish) is never
        included in the index. It is silently dropped on the next append or on
        recovery; the journal remains consistent with the longest prefix of
        fully-written frames.
  INV7. The index is rebuilt atomically: a new index is constructed in memory
        from the verified frames and only then swapped in. Partial/old state is
        never observed by a concurrent reader of the index.
  INV8. Offsets stored in the index are absolute file offsets into the journal
        file. This lets `read_at(offset)` be implemented without re-scanning.

# durable_event_journal.py
"""
Durable append-only event journal.

DESIGN INVARIANTS (documented so future maintainers don't break them):

I1. Framing is self-delimiting. Every record in the file is written as:
        <length: 4 bytes big-endian uint32> <payload: length bytes> <crc32: 4 bytes>
    A reader can walk the whole file using only these three fields WITHOUT
    consulting any external index. This is the property that makes recovery
    possible after a partial write.

I2. The length field is written *first*, then payload, then checksum. A torn
    write can therefore only leave the file in one of these states:
        - 0 bytes of the frame (nothing happened)
        - 1..3 bytes of the length prefix (we can detect the short prefix)
        - length prefix complete, payload short (we know how much is missing)
        - payload complete, checksum short (we recompute or reject)
    These are the ONLY truncation shapes a crash can produce. Recovery below
    handles all of them explicitly; anything else would violate I1.

I3. Checksum covers the payload only (not the length). This keeps the CRC
    computation cheap and the length-prefix invariant independent. The length
    is validated structurally by the reader; the checksum validates semantics.

I4. fsync is required after every append for durability. Without fsync, a
    successful write() may still be lost on power failure. Append() MUST NOT
    return before the frame is on stable storage. The flush() in older code
    was insufficient; we use os.fsync / fdatasync.

I5. Index is derived state. The in-memory index (offset, length, crc, kind)
    may be rebuilt from the file at any time. It is never authoritative; the
    file is. Any disagreement between file and index is resolved in favor of
    the file (the index is discarded and rebuilt).

I6. Append-only contract. We never overwrite or mutate an existing byte in
    the file. Rebuilding, filtering, and recovery only append or truncate a
    trailing partial frame. Truncation cuts only the incomplete tail.

I7. Single writer. Concurrency between writers is not supported at the
    library level; the caller must serialize appends. Reader windows during
    append are safe

# Design Review: Island Microgrid — Solar, Wind, Battery, and Backup Generation

## 1. Scope and Operating Philosophy

This review examines the design of an island microgrid comprising photovoltaic (PV) generation, wind turbines, a battery energy storage system (BESS), and backup diesel or dual-fuel generators. The central operating invariant is instantaneous power balance: at every control interval, aggregate generation must equal aggregate load plus losses, with the BESS absorbing or supplying the differential within its state-of-charge (SOC) limits. Because the island has no mainland interconnection, there is no infinite bus to lean on; reliability must be engineered into the system through reserve capacity, redundancy, and controlled mode transitions rather than borrowed from a larger grid. The review treats the microgrid as a cyber-physical system in which scheduling, forecasting, protection, and measurement are interdependent, and it evaluates each of those layers against the operating invariant and the reliability requirement it serves.

The design philosophy adopted here is "forecast-driven scheduling with hard physical fallbacks." Forecasting and optimization determine the economically preferred operating point; physical reserves, SOC bounds, and generator readiness determine the admissible operating envelope. When the two disagree — as they inevitably will during forecast errors and seasonal extremes — the physical envelope takes precedence and the scheduler is re-run. This hierarchy matters because a microgrid that optimizes aggressively into a thin reserve margin will fail on the first significant forecast miss, whereas one that optimizes within a conservative envelope degrades gracefully.

## 2. Architecture and Dispatch Layers

The design uses a three-layer dispatch hierarchy. The top layer is a day-ahead and intra-day scheduler that produces a unit commitment and an economic dispatch plan over rolling 24-hour and 4-hour horizons at 15-minute resolution. The middle layer is a real-time dispatch engine operating at 1-second to 1-minute resolution that enforces power balance, SOC limits, and reserve constraints, and issues setpoints to PV inverters (curtailment or MPPT), wind converters (curtailment), the BESS power conversion system (PCS), and generators (start/stop and load level). This review evaluates the design of an islanded electrical microgrid intended to serve a remote island community with no submarine cable connection to a mainland grid. The generation portfolio comprises solar photovoltaic (PV) arrays, wind turbines, a battery energy storage system (BESS), and diesel or dual-fuel backup generators. The review covers real-time balance of supply and demand, battery state-of-charge (SOC) constraints, forecast uncertainty, reserve margins, seasonal variability, islanded-mode transitions, maintenance, and the measurement and verification plan. The following design review evaluates the proposed island microgrid architecture, which integrates solar photovoltaic (PV) generation, wind turbine generation, battery energy storage systems (BESS), and backup diesel or gas generators. The central operational imperative is instantaneous supply-demand balance, a constraint that governs every aspect of the design from component sizing to control logic. Because the system is islanded—meaning it has no external grid interconnection to absorb or supply deficits—the microgrid must function as a self-contained frequency and voltage reference. This review addresses scheduling algorithms, reserve margin philosophy, forecasting error management, seasonal variability, maintenance regimes, and measurement and verification plans. Each section identifies design strengths, exposes risk areas, and recommends specific engineering measures to close gaps.

**1. System Architecture and Instantaneous Balance Requirement**

The microgrid topology should be explicitly defined before any scheduling logic is developed. A recommended architecture comprises a set of distributed PV inverters and wind turbine converters feeding a common AC bus, a central BESS connected through a bidirectional power conversion system (PCS), and one or more backup generator sets with automatic transfer and paralleling capability. The control hierarchy should be layered: a primary layer operating at sub-second timescales for voltage and frequency regulation, a secondary layer at seconds-to-minutes for power sharing and reserve activation, and a tertiary layer at minutes-to-hours for economic and reliability-oriented scheduling.

Instantaneous balance is not merely a planning objective; it is a physical law. In an islanded AC system, any mismatch between generation and load manifests as a deviation in bus frequency (for grid-forming sources) or bus voltage collapse. The design must therefore specify which assets are grid-forming and which are grid-following. A robust choice is to designate the BESS PCS as the primary grid-forming unit, with at least one backup generator capable of assuming grid-forming duty during BESS unavailability or depletion. PV and wind converters operate as grid-following sources, injecting power according to availability and curtailment commands. This hierarchy ensures a continuous reference for frequency and voltage even when renewable output collapses.

A critical design point is droop control tuning on the grid-forming BESS. Frequency droop and voltage droop coefficients must be coordinated with generator governor settings so that load sharing between BESS and generators is predictable and stable. Improper droop coordination can cause hunting between sources, transient frequency excursions, or unintended reverse power flow into generators. The review recommends simulation-based validation of droop settings across the full range of load steps, renewable ramps, and generator start sequences.

#
# DESIGN OVERVIEW
# ================
#
# We store events in a single append-only file.  Each event is wrapped in a
# "frame" consisting of:
#
#     [4-byte big-endian length L] [L bytes payload] [4-byte CRC32 checksum]
#
# The length prefix describes ONLY the payload, not the checksum.  The
# checksum is computed over the payload bytes (encode_event output).
#
# INVARIANTS
# ----------
#
# I1. A frame is only considered "valid" iff:
#       - its length prefix can be read,
#       - the payload bytes are all present,
#       - the trailing checksum bytes are all present,
#       - the stored checksum equals crc32(payload).
#
# I2. The journal file always begins with valid frames, optionally followed by
#     at most one partial ("torn") frame at the tail.  We never write garbage
#     in the middle of the file: appends are strictly monotonic, and torn
#     frames only occur at the end (e.g. process crash mid-write).
#
# I3. Recovery truncates the file at the offset just past the last valid
#     frame.  This guarantees I2 again after recovery.
#
# I4. The in-memory index (event_id -> file offset, length) is rebuilt by
#     scanning valid frames.  The index is committed atomically: we build a
#     brand-new index object and swap it in only after the scan completes
#     without error, so readers either see the old index or the new one,
#     never a half-populated index.
#
# I5. Readers ignore torn tail frames (they're beyond the valid region).
#
# I6. Writes are crash-safe at the *frame* granularity when the underlying
#     filesystem respects `flush()`.  We do NOT promise atomicity for the
#     user's business logic, only for framing integrity.
#
# I7. The length prefix is capped at MAX_PAYLOAD so a corrupt prefix cannot

## 1. Introduction and Scope

This review examines an islanded (isolated, non-grid-tied) electrical microgrid comprising solar photovoltaic (PV) generation, wind turbines, a battery energy storage system (BESS), and backup diesel or gas generators. The stated operational premises are fourfold: supply and demand must balance at every instant; battery state of charge (SOC) is bounded; forecasts carry uncertainty; and reliability depends on independent reserves plus safe transitions between operating modes. Each of these premises is simultaneously a constraint, a design driver, and a source of failure modes, and the review treats them as such rather than as textbook assumptions. The island setting sharpens every issue: there is no utility interconnection to absorb a deficit or dump a surplus, so the microgrid must be self-sufficient across timescales ranging from millisecond transients to seasonal adequacy.

The review covers scheduling architecture, reserve margin philosophy, forecasting error treatment, seasonal effects, maintenance strategy, and measurement/verification plans. It is written as a critique of design choices and their interactions, with explicit attention to where subsystems couple and where independence is claimed but not delivered.

## 2. System Description and Load Characterization

The generation portfolio is a mixed inverter-based resource: PV arrays (likely distributed across rooftops or ground mounts), horizontal- or vertical-axis wind turbines, a lithium-ion or flow BESS, and one or more synchronous or inverter-coupled backup generators. The load is assumed to be a mixed island community load with residential, commercial, water pumping, and possibly desalination components — the latter is important because desalination and pumping loads are large, deferrable, and unusually well-suited to demand-side scheduling.

A critical design question arises immediately: what is the load's tolerated voltage and frequency envelope, and what fraction of load is sheddable under contract? The design must classify loads into tiers (critical, interruptible, deferrable, discretionary) and encode this classification in both the scheduling layer and the protection scheme. # durable_event_journal.py
"""
A durable, append-only event journal for Python.

Design overview
---------------
The journal stores *events* as framed records on disk. Each frame is:

    [ 4-byte big-endian length of payload ]
    [ payload bytes (opaque, produced by encode_event) ]
    [ 4-byte big-endian CRC32 of payload bytes ]

We use CRC32 for integrity checks because it is cheap, standard, and
sufficient to detect the kinds of corruption that happen during crashes
(partial writes, torn sectors, media glitches). Checksums are computed
over the payload only -- not over the length prefix -- so that a corrupted
length cannot silently shift the interpretation of a "valid" checksum.

Invariants maintained by this module
------------------------------------
I1. Frame layout: every *committed* frame is exactly
    L bytes of length prefix (4) + N payload bytes + 4 bytes of CRC.
    The writer writes the length prefix, payload and CRC in that order
    and flushes the OS buffer after every append to guarantee that once
    append() returns successfully the frame is durable up to fsync()

I2. Append order: `_offset` is monotonically increasing within a single
    writer. Two writers on the same file are illegal (documented, not
    prevented) -- callers must acquire an exclusive lock (see FileLock)
    and this module assumes they do.

I3. Recovery: after a crash, the tail of the file may contain zero or
    more *partial* frames. On open() we scan frames forward and stop at
    the first frame that fails a *structural* check (L or CRC). All bytes
    after the last valid frame boundary are truncated before the journal
    becomes usable again. Truncation is atomic in the sense of: we
    write a new EOF marker? No -- we simply truncate(). See comments
    below on the TOCTOU safety of truncate().

I4. Index rebuild: the in-memory index maps "logical offset" (index of
    the frame in the stream, 0-based) to "physical byte offset". We
    rebuild it deterministically on open(). The index is derivable from
    the bytes on disk; we therefore do not persist it. This avoids a
    second source of truth and means recovery after tail corruption
    never leaves a stale index pointing

# Design Review: Island Microgrid — Solar, Wind, Battery, and Backup Generation

## 1. Scope and Operating Context

This review addresses a stand-alone island microgrid with four supply resources: photovoltaic (PV) generation, wind turbines, a battery energy storage system (BESS), and backup diesel or dual-fuel generators. The system serves an islanded load with no synchronous interconnection to a mainland grid, so the microgrid must form its own voltage and frequency reference and must balance supply and demand continuously. The review covers: (a) dispatch and scheduling architecture; (b) reserve margins and their independence; (c) treatment of forecast uncertainty; (d) seasonal and inter-annual variability; (e) maintenance planning and asset management; and (f) the measurement and instrumentation plan needed to validate all of the above.

The island context imposes several constraints that dominate the design. First, the renewable resource is variable and partially correlated with load in the case of PV (daytime air-conditioning and commercial load) but weakly correlated in the case of wind. Second, fuel logistics are expensive and weather-dependent; generator fuel must be shipped and stored on-island, which raises the cost of every liter burned for reserve or standby. Third, the absence of a bulk grid means there is no external source of inertia or frequency support during contingencies. Fourth, island loads often exhibit strong seasonal patterns (tourism, agriculture, fishing, water pumping) and may be dominated by a few large customers whose behavior is not statistically smooth. Fifth, maintenance access is limited by weather windows and by the small pool of qualified technicians, making planned outages and spare-parts logistics a first-order design variable rather than an afterthought.

The review is organized around a layered control architecture: a long-horizon scheduler (day-ahead and multi-day), an intra-day rolling dispatch layer, a real-time balancing layer operating on seconds-to-minutes, and a protection and mode-management layer operating on milliseconds-to-seconds. Each layer has distinct timescales, distinct uncertainty sources, and distinct reserve requirements. A common failure mode in island microgrids is conflation of these layers — using the day-ahead schedule as if it were a real-time guarantee, or sizing reserves at the scheduling layer without accounting for the faster layers' needs.

# Design Review: Island Microgrid — Solar, Wind, Storage, and Backup Generation

## 1. Scope and Operating Philosophy

This review evaluates the design of an islanded microgrid intended to serve a permanent population with critical loads (water pumping, communications, clinic refrigeration) and general commercial/residential demand. Generation assets are solar photovoltaic (PV), wind turbines, a battery energy storage system (BESS), and Diesel or dual-fuel backup generators. There is no utility interconnection; the island grid is the only source of power, so every design decision must be judged against a single non-negotiable criterion: **the instantaneous balance of supply and demand must hold at all times, under all forecast conditions, across all seasons, and through all maintenance states.**

The design follows a layered defense model:

- **Layer 1 — Real-time balancing:** primary inverter-based control (grid-forming storage or a master inverter) maintains voltage and frequency and absorbs the sub-second mismatch between renewable output and load.
- **Layer 2 — Minute-to-hour scheduling:** an energy management system (EMS) commits dispatchable assets (BESS charge/discharge, generator start/stop) against rolling forecasts.
- **Layer 3 — Reserve capacity:** scheduled reserves cover forecast error, forced outages, and load surprises; reserves are separated into spinning (online) and non-spinning (standby) categories.
- **Layer 4 — Emergency:** under-frequency/over-frequency load shedding, generator fast-start, and controlled brownout sequences for non-critical circuits.

Each layer must be independently sufficient to prevent a cascading failure; the design is reviewed below for whether that independence is actually achieved.

## 2. Architecture and Asset Sizing

### 2.1 Generation Mix

The PV array is the largest energy source on most days, with a peak DC rating sized to cover midday commercial load plus BESS charging. Wind contributes a smaller but complementary profile: on this island the wind resource peaks in the evening and overnight, partially decorrelating from solar and reducing the evening ramp that would otherwise fall entirely on the BESS and generators.
